title: Transfer Functions, Poles and Zeros
question: Can we read a system's whole personality off one fraction?

blocks.text: Start the drone hovering at 1 m, with 4.9 N of base thrust balancing gravity. Measure both the requested change and the actual height change from that baseline. Just before a new request, both changes are zero. In the step example the request jumps to 2 m at $t=0$, so its change becomes 1 m while the drone is still at 1 m.
Good, because last chapter we dropped the $-h(0)$ bits and the formula lied. Measured from the hover, those starting values really **are** zero, so this time they vanish honestly.

Hover thrust cancels gravity, so only the *changes* are left in the drone's equation. Now use Chapter 7's rule: every slope becomes × $s$, minus its starting value. From the hover every starting value is zero, so nothing is subtracted:

blocks.tex: \begin{gathered} m\,\Delta\out{h}'' + c\,\Delta\out{h}' = \eff{K_p}\,(\Delta\sp{r} - \Delta\out{h}) \\[2pt] \Big\downarrow\ {\scriptstyle \Delta h(0)\,=\,\Delta h'(0)\,=\,0} \\[2pt] (m s^2 + c s + \eff{K_p})\,\Delta\out{H}(s) = \eff{K_p}\,\Delta\sp{R}(s) \end{gathered}

blocks.text: Divide by $m s^2 + c s + \eff{K_p}$ and there is $G(s)$. Its bottom is the very equation we got in Chapters 4 to 6 by guessing $e^{st}$.
So it's not magic. It's the drone's own equation, with every slope turned into an $s$.

$\Delta\sp{R}(s)$ is the transform of the **requested change** from 1 m; $\Delta\out{H}(s)$ is the transform of the **actual change** from 1 m. $G(s)$ is fixed by the drone and controller. It is the **transfer function**: output change divided by input change, with both changes starting at zero.
The plot still shows heights above the ground. Add the 1 m starting height to a change predicted by the formula to get the blue height on the plot.
June was right: the fraction **is** the drone. It's like its **recipe**. Feed in any ingredient and it tells you what comes out!
Try three different inputs on the same drone. The recipe never changes, only $\Delta\sp{R}(s)$ does.

items.def: Transformed output change ÷ transformed input change, starting from the same resting state. For this linear drone it is a fraction of polynomials in $s$.
Every change and its speed is zero at $t = 0$, as when we measure from the hover. Then Chapter 7's starting-value terms like $-h(0)$ are zero too, and $G(s)$ is the whole story.

sections.title: Poles: where the system wants to live

blocks.text: Where does $G(s)$ **blow up**? Where its denominator is zero. Those points are the **poles**, drawn as ×. In this drone there are two, one for each of the two natural $e^{st}$ motions from Chapter 6.
In Chapter 7, the transform of $e^{at}$ screamed at $s = a$. Read it backwards: wherever $G$ screams, a motion $e^{pt}$ is hiding.
So the poles are Chapter 6's **modes**, sitting on the map!

A step response is $G(s)$ times the step's $\frac{1}{s}$. Split it into simple pieces, as Chapter 7 did: the step's own pole at 0 gives the final change $A$, and each pole of $G$ gives one piece $\frac{B}{s-p}$.

blocks.tex: \begin{aligned} \Delta\out{H}(s) = G(s)\cdot\frac{1}{s} &= \frac{A}{s} + \frac{B}{s-p} + \frac{\bar B}{s-\bar p} \\[4pt] \Longrightarrow\quad \Delta\out{h}(t) &= A + B e^{pt} + \bar B e^{\bar p t} \end{aligned}

blocks.text: Chapter 7's table turns each piece back into a motion. Nothing else can appear: the poles are the whole cast.
And a pole with $\sigma > 0$ is a piece that grows. No wonder the right half blows up.

Now flip it around. Instead of choosing gains and finding the poles, let's **drag the poles** and see what drone we get. That needs a second knob, $\eff{K_d}$: a push against speed, which we'll meet properly in Chapter 9. It adds to the drag $c$, and the two roots are $p$ and its mirror twin $\bar p$ (the bar flips the sign of the imaginary part, like Chapter 5's twins):

blocks.tex: \begin{aligned} & m s^2 + (c + \eff{K_d})\,s + \eff{K_p} = 0 \\ \Longrightarrow\quad & s = p,\ \bar p \qquad \text{(the poles)} \end{aligned}

blocks.text: To put the poles at −{scrub|sig} ± {scrub|w}i, the controller needs $\eff{K_p} = m(\sigma^2+\omega^2)$ = {calc|kp|eff} N/m and $c + \eff{K_d} = 2m|\sigma|$ = {calc|damp} N·s/m, so $\eff{K_d}$ = {calc|kd|eff} N·s/m. The playground below follows these numbers. {calc|note}

blocks.q: What does the drone do if we drag the poles into the **right half** of the s-plane?

options.why: Landing needs everything to calm down, and right-half poles do the opposite.
Steady wobbling is what you get exactly **on** the vertical axis. Just past it, things grow.

options.text: It swings harder and harder until it crashes or flies off
options.why: On the right half, $e^{st}$ has $\sigma > 0$: a growing spiral. The swings get bigger every cycle.

blocks.text: Reading the map
Play with it. A few rules jump out, and each one is an old friend in disguise:

items: **Left half = calms down, right half = blows up.** The real part $\sigma$ is the shrink or grow rate of $e^{\sigma t}$.

**Further left = faster.** Settling takes about $4/|\sigma|$ seconds (the dashed vertical lines): Chapter 6's four time constants, since $e^{-|\sigma| t}$ is below 2 % after $\ln 50/|\sigma| \approx 3.9/|\sigma|$ seconds.
**Further up = more wiggly.** The height $\omega$ is Chapter 6's damped frequency, so one wiggle takes $2\pi/\omega$ seconds.

**The angle sets the overshoot.** The angle $\theta$ from the negative real axis gives $\zeta = \cos\theta$ (Chapter 6's circle), and the overshoot is $e^{-\pi|\sigma|/\omega}$ (the dashed rays). Near the real axis it barely overshoots, near the vertical axis a lot.

blocks.text: I wanted just **one** pole up high and one down low. It won't let me! The bottom one keeps copying the top one.
Remember the twin spinners from Chapter 5? A real drone has real motion, so every spinning $e^{st}$ needs its mirror twin to cancel the imaginary parts. Complex poles **always** come in mirror pairs.

blocks.title: Why the angle sets the overshoot

blocks.text: The drone passes the target and turns round after half a wiggle, at $t = \pi/\omega$. By then the shrinking $e^{-|\sigma| t}$ has been at work for that long, and what's left of the swing is the overshoot. Only the ratio $|\sigma|/\omega$ matters, and that ratio is the pole's *angle*. On Chapter 6's circle, the cosine of that angle is $\zeta$.

Poles at −{scrub|sig} ± {scrub|w}i: the wiggles shrink like $e^{-|\sigma| t}$, so it settles in about {calc|ts} s. One wiggle takes {calc|period} s. The first peak comes after half of one, at {calc|tp} s, and by then the shrinking has left an overshoot of {calc|os}.
So every ray from 0 is one $\zeta$, and one overshoot.

blocks.q: Keep $\sigma = -2$ and slide the poles **straight up**, from $\pm 4i$ to $\pm 8i$. What changes?

options.why: Settling follows the shrink rate $\sigma$, which didn't move. Measured: 1.87 s becomes 1.72 s, nearly the same.

options.text: Faster wiggles and more overshoot; settling stays about the same
options.why: One wiggle drops from 1.57 s to 0.79 s and the overshoot rises from 21 % to 46 %, but the envelope $e^{-2t}$ is unchanged, so settling stays near $4/2 = 2$ s.
Only the left-right position decides that. Up and down never crosses into the right half.

blocks.text: The playground jumped when we answered: the ghost pair sits at $\pm 4i$, the new one at $\pm 8i$. Same envelope, twice as many wiggles, and a much bigger first swing.
Our drone started at $-1 \pm 6.24i$: that's the $K_p = 20$ drone from Chapter 2. Far up (very wiggly) and close to the axis (slow to settle). Now you can *see* why it bounced.
What if both poles sit on the real axis, one at $-0.2$ and one at $-5$?
The fast one's gone in a second. The slow one is the boss.

Real poles at −0.2 and −5. After {scrub|time} s, the fast motion $e^{-5t}$ has {calc|fast} of its start left, and the slow one $e^{-0.2t}$ still has {calc|slow}. So the slow pole decides: settling takes about $4/0.2 = 20$ s.

items.def: A value of $s$ where the transfer function blows up. Each pole $p$ is one motion $e^{pt}$ of the system.
Two poles with the same real part and opposite imaginary parts. Complex poles of a real system always come this way.
The pole nearest the vertical axis. Its slow motion outlasts the others, so it decides the settling time.

blocks.text: Four is Chapter 6's $\ln 50 \approx 3.9$, rounded: the time for the *envelope* to shrink to 2 %. The real curve sits inside its envelope, so it often settles a bit sooner. It settles later when the poles sit on or near the real axis, because a double pole has a $t\,e^{-|\sigma| t}$ part that lingers.
I tried $\sigma = -1$: the rule said 4 s, and the real times ran from 3.0 s to 5.8 s depending on $\zeta$. Good enough to aim with, not good enough to promise.

The numerator can be zero too. Those points are **zeros**, drawn as ○. Usually they change **how much** of each pole's motion appears in the output. If a zero sits exactly on a pole, the shared factor cancels and that pole disappears from this input-to-output recipe.

Here's a system with fixed poles at $-2 \pm 3i$ and one zero you can slide. (Our playground's $\eff{K_d}$ pushes against the drone's *speed*, so its recipe has no zero. Push against the *error's* speed instead, as Chapter 9 will, and a zero appears at $-\eff{K_p}/\eff{K_d}$: for these poles that's $-6.5$, with 15 % overshoot instead of 12 %.)
Same poles, but when the zero gets close to the origin the response jumps up way faster and overshoots more!
Same poles means the same motions. So the zero can't add a new one. It must be adding a bit of something we already have.
With the zero at −{scrub|z}, the output is the no-zero curve **plus {calc|gain} × its slope**, and it overshoots by {calc|os} (12% without the zero).

Multiplying by $s$ takes the slope (Chapter 7), so the factor $(1 + s/|z|)$ adds $1/|z|$ times the slope. That's why a zero near the origin makes the system react so strongly to **changes**: the overshoot grows, even though the poles didn't move. Far away, the zero hardly matters. That's all we need about zeros for now.

A pole is a motion the system *makes*; a zero is a motion it *refuses to pass on*. Feed this system (zero at $-3$) exactly $e^{-3t}$ and none of it comes out: only the system's own wiggle, which dies away. Without the zero, $1.3\,e^{-3t}$ would come straight through.
Like noise-cancelling headphones for one particular hum.

items.def: A value of $s$ where the transfer function is zero: a motion $e^{zt}$ the system does not pass on.

blocks.text: Easy: drag the poles *way* left. Settles in a blink. Best drone ever!
What thrust does that need, though? Until now we've pretended the motors could push as hard as the maths wants.

Time to be honest. Our motors can push between **0 N** and **20 N** (about four times the drone's weight). Below, the poles move left along a 45° line (that's $\zeta \approx 0.71$, Chapter 6's sweet spot). The dashed curves are the maths with imaginary, unlimited motors; the solid ones are real motors.

At the first instant of a 1 m step the error is the whole metre and the drone isn't moving yet, so the maths asks for hover plus $\eff{K_p}$ × 1 m. With the poles at {scrub|sig} that's {calc|sum|eff} N: {calc|verdict}.

Past about $-3.9 \pm 3.9i$ the maths asks for more than 20 N. The {eff|orange thrust} flattens against the limit, and past about $-6 \pm 6i$ the maths even wants to pull the drone *down*, which propellers can't. The real drone stops following the pretty linear prediction. Its settling stops improving at about 0.7 s, near $-6.5 \pm 6.5i$, and further left it gets *worse*, with extra overshoot.
I slid it all the way to $-8 \pm 8i$. The maths says 0.53 s. The real drone takes 0.77 s: slower than at $-6.5$!
And its overshoot went from 4 % to 16 %. All that extra thrust was never there to be had.
So "further left" is only better until you run out of motor. Placing poles is a trade-off, not a race.

blocks.title: A thrust budget is a circle

blocks.text: At the very first instant the drone hasn't moved, so only $\eff{K_p}$ pushes, and $\eff{K_p} = m|p|^2$: the square of the poles' distance from 0. Double the distance and you need four times the push, whichever direction you went. For a 1 m step our motors allow poles out to about 5.5 from 0 (the faint orange circle in the playground). Ask for a 2 m step and the circle shrinks to 3.9.
For a {scrub|dr} m step, the first push stays under 20 N only if the poles sit within {calc|r} of 0, in any direction.
From now on the 20 N limit stays switched on.

items.def: The thrust asked for at the first instant of a step: $mg + \eff{K_p}\,\Delta r$, before the drone has moved.
The pole positions the motors can afford for a given step: a circle around 0.
Real thrust is clipped to 0–20 N, whatever the maths asks for.

items: Yes, one fraction does it. The **transfer function** $G(s)$ = output change ÷ input change in s-land, starting from rest. It's the system's recipe, $\Delta\out{H} = G\cdot\Delta\sp{R}$, and it comes straight from the drone's equation.
**Poles** (×) are where $G(s)$ explodes: the $e^{pt}$ modes the system is made of.

Left half = stable, right half = explodes. Further left = faster (settles in about $4/|\sigma|$ s, a rule of thumb), higher = wigglier (one wiggle = $2\pi/\omega$ s), angle = damping $\zeta$ = overshoot $e^{-\pi|\sigma|/\omega}$. The pole nearest the axis is the boss.
Complex poles always come in mirror pairs.
**Zeros** (○) change how much of each mode you get. Near the origin they add a kick: $1/|z|$ times the slope.
The first push is $mg + m|p|^2$ for a 1 m step, so far-away poles need thrust the motors don't have.

options.why: Settling ≈ $4/1 = 4$ s. The height (2) only affects wiggling, not settling.
High up means lots of fast wiggles, but it's close to the axis, so they die out slowly (≈ 8 s).

items.q: $G(s) = \dfrac{3}{s^2 + 2s + 10}$. Where are the poles, and what does the response look like?

options.why: $s = \frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 40}}{2} = -1 \pm 3i$. Left half means stable, imaginary part means wiggles.
Sign slip. For $s^2 + bs + q$ the real part is $-b/2 = -1$, which is in the left half.
Those are just coefficients of the polynomial. The poles are its roots: $-1 \pm 3i$.

items.q: You want **less overshoot** but the **same settling time**. How do you move the poles?

options.text: Straight towards the real axis (keep σ, shrink ω)
options.why: Same distance from the axis keeps the *envelope* the same, so settling stays about the same (the $4/|\sigma|$ rule; it's rough near the real axis). A smaller angle from the real axis means more damping, so less overshoot.
That swings the angle towards the vertical axis: *more* overshoot and faster wiggles.
That makes it settle more slowly, and past the axis it becomes unstable.

items.q: A system has real poles at $-0.2$ and $-5$. After two seconds, which one is still shaping the response?

options.text: The one at $-0.2$, near the axis
options.why: $e^{-0.2t}$ is still at 67 % after 2 s; $e^{-5t}$ is down to 0.005 %. The slow pole is in charge, so settling takes about $4/0.2 = 20$ s.
Further left means it dies *faster*. After just 1 s it's below 1 % of its start (0.67 %).
One shrinks 25 times faster than the other ($5 \div 0.2$). After half a second the fast one is at 8 %, the slow one still at 90 %.

blocks.text: Theo: "The poles are beautiful. But hold on: we cheated all chapter by handing the drone its hover thrust. Without it, gravity still makes it **droop**. Our map is fine. It's our *controller* that needs fixing."

recipe.title: One recipe, three inputs
recipe.plotAria: Setpoint and drone height over time for the chosen input.

describe.step: The setpoint steps from 1 to 2 metres and the drone follows with a bouncy overshoot.
describe.pulse: The setpoint glides from 1 to 2 metres; the drone follows with a smaller bounce.
describe.wave: The setpoint waves up and down; the drone follows the wave.

status.step: It overshoots to {p} m before it settles at 2 m.
status.pulse: A softer start: it only peaks at {p} m.
status.wave: The recipe turns a {a} m wave into a {b} m wave.

playground.title: The pole playground
playground.planeAria: The s-plane with a draggable pair of poles. Left half calms down, right half blows up. Use arrow keys to move the selected pole.
playground.plotAria: Step response of the drone for the chosen poles, previous response shown as a ghost.

verdict.marginal: Right on the axis: it swings forever.
verdict.hitPage: It flew out of its picture, hit the page, and fell. Move a pole to try again.
verdict.hitGround: It crashed into the ground. Move a pole to try again.
verdict.hitPageMarginal: Each swing reached 3 m, just enough to touch the page; the motors stalled and it fell.

playground.negKd: Kd is negative here: the drag already damps more than these poles allow, so the controller has to push along with the motion.
playground.pushWarn: The first push is over 20 N, more than real motors have. We’ll see what that costs in a moment.
playground.challenge: Mini-challenge: overshoot under 10% and settled within 2 s
playground.chalOk: Challenge met! Overshoot {o}%, settled in {s} s.
playground.chalNo: Not yet: overshoot {o}%, settles in {s} s. Aim for the highlighted zone.
playground.help: Drag either × (or Tab to it and use the arrow keys, Shift for big steps). The drone replays its step response each time.
playground.describe: Poles at {p}. Damping ratio {z}. Settles in about {s} seconds, overshoots about {o} percent.

zero.title: Slide the zero

zero.note: Zero at {z}; scaled so it still ends at 1.
zero.near: Near the origin: the slope part is {g} × the old slope, so the start kicks hard.
zero.far: Far away: only {g} × the slope. It hardly shows.
zero.help: Drag the ○ along the axis (or Tab to it and use ← →). The × poles stay put.

limit.title: Real motors have limits
limit.hAria: Height after a step for unlimited and for real motors.
limit.tAria: Thrust over time, with the 0 and 20 newton motor limits.
limit.capped: The maths wants {p} N; the motors stop at 20 N. Real settling {s} s, and no amount of “further left” gets it under about {b} s.
limit.fantasy: Imaginary motors happily deliver {p} N. Switch the limits back on.
